dietEvidence.body: The dentition is consistent with carnivory. No gut contents or direct feeding traces are known for Acrocanthosaurus, so prey choice and hunting method are inferred from anatomy and from other large theropods.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A large carcharodontosaurid with tall neural spines along the back. The spines supported a ridge of muscle and skin, not a sail like Spinosaurus.
summary: Acrocanthosaurus atokensis is a large carcharodontosaurid from the Aptian–Albian of the southern Western Interior. It is known from a partial type skeleton and referred skull and postcranial material. The tall neural spines supported a muscle-and-skin ridge, not a thin sail, and its forelimb function is reconstructed rather than observed.

discovery.body: Named by Stovall & Langston, 1950. The record is known from Antlers Formation, Oklahoma and Texas. Several partial skeletons, including a nearly complete specimen from Oklahoma.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Several partial skeletons, including a nearly complete specimen from Oklahoma.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Antlers Formation, Oklahoma and Texas records the species in the Early Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈115–110 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

fossilEvidence.title: Type and referred material
fossilEvidence.body: The holotype is a partial skeleton from the Antlers Formation. Referred skull and postcranial specimens add anatomy, but the species is not known from a complete skeleton. The neural-spine ridge is reconstructed from the preserved vertebrae.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The dorsal neural spines are elongated but not as extreme as those of Spinosaurus; the skull is large and lightly built.

behaviour.body: The behavioural evidence is skeletal: the tall neural spines are consistent with a display or muscle-support ridge, but the soft tissue is unknown. Forelimb range of motion is compatible with grasping, not proof of a particular hunting strategy. No bonebed or trackway establishes social behaviour.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from several partial skeletons, including a nearly complete specimen from Oklahoma. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The type is incomplete, but referred skull and postcranial material make the species anatomically well known. The soft tissue over the neural spines is not preserved, and the forelimb’s role in hunting is inferred from joint mechanics.
